findings.headline: Council tax collection rates declining in Dacorum amid household financial vulnerability.
findings.detail: Dacorum is one of only two Hertfordshire districts with declining council tax collection rates in 2025/26, with a 0.1 percentage point year-on-year decrease. The council identifies household financial vulnerability as the cause, noting that struggling households may deprioritise council tax behind utilities and food. Council tax retention of £16.186m (from £191m collected across preceptors) represents 11% of baseline revenue funding.
findings.matters: Declining tax collection reduces actual revenue below forecasts and signals emerging household financial stress that could spread across other councils.
findings.figures: 0.1% collection rate decline, £16.186m retained by council, £191m total collected
findings.quote: During 2025/26 in year Council tax collection rates across Hertfordshire are improved year on year for 6 out of the 10 districts, with Dacorum one of two authorities that has a slight reduction of 0.1% in the collection rates year on year.

findings.headline: 2027/28 budget balance depends on £900k in unproven efficiencies and income that council flags as at-risk.
findings.detail: The 2027/28 budget requires £900k in new savings and income (£865k income generation plus £269k service efficiencies) to meet an £867k savings requirement. The income comprises £500k treasury investment returns (contingent on sustained high interest rates), £300k planning fee improvements, and commercial income growth. The council explicitly states these targets are "projected but remain at risk until budget setting and financial approval." Failure to deliver would leave a funding gap of £867k.
findings.matters: Savings plans flagged at-risk but essential to balance the budget indicate execution risk; non-delivery would force mid-year service cuts or reserve drawdown.
findings.figures: £867k savings requirement, £900k efficiency/income target (£865k income + £269k efficiencies), £500k treasury income assumption
findings.quote: £900k of income/savings efficiencies are projected in the MTFS as outlined in section 5.3. These are projected but remain at risk until budget setting and financial approval.

findings.paper_title: FINAL - Appendix A Quarterly Strategic Risk update Q4 2526
findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation creating structural change with undefined transition costs ahead of July 2026 government decision
findings.detail: Dacorum is part of a 12-council Hertfordshire devolution and reorganisation proposal submitted to government in November 2025, with a decision expected July 2026. The council acknowledges that future transition work must address system standardisation, partnership reshaping, savings realisation, and operational protocols, but these have not yet been fully defined or costed.
findings.matters: Major institutional restructuring creates execution and financial risk; a lender must assess whether this will require additional borrowing or will consume resources that could otherwise support debt service.
findings.figures: 12 Hertfordshire councils involved in proposal; government decision expected July 2026
findings.quote: Future work will need to consider areas such as standardising systems, reshaping partnerships, delivering savings, and preparing transition protocols. Work is actively underway now to plan transition work ahead of an expected government decision in July 2026.

findings.paper_title: FINAL - Appendix A Quarterly Strategic Risk update Q4 2526
findings.headline: Housing Revenue Account under pressure from significant damp and mould compliance costs alongside inflationary maintenance demand
findings.detail: The HRA faces two concurrent cost pressures: significant compliance costs for damp and mould remediation (driven by regulatory requirements), and inflationary pressures plus increased repairs and maintenance demand. The council states these pressures are currently being mitigated within HRA income streams but require ongoing monitoring.
findings.matters: The HRA is a material part of the council's financial position; if these cost pressures exceed projections, it could constrain cash reserves and borrowing flexibility.
findings.figures: HRA improved in-year surplus reported in 2025/26; £3.8m grant for Warm Homes Social Housing Wave 3 with 91 properties planned
findings.quote: There remains significant service pressures related damp and mould work but at present these are being mitigated and supported by the HRA income streams. The HRA is impacted significantly by inflationary cost pressures and increased demand relating to repairs and maintenance.

findings.paper_title: FINAL - Appendix A Quarterly Strategic Risk update Q4 2526
findings.headline: £2.1m in unidentified savings still required to meet the medium-term financial strategy
findings.detail: The council's 2026/27 budget is balanced in plan, but meeting this depends on achieving £2.1m in savings over the MTFS period that have not yet been identified. The council is developing the 2026 MTFS to outline a sustainable medium-term financial plan.
findings.matters: A lender assessing borrowing capacity must understand whether a balanced budget is built on identified reductions or unproven efficiency gains; unidentified savings represent planning and delivery risk.
findings.figures: £2.1m unidentified savings requirement; 2025/26 reported overall surplus and 2026/27 projected balanced position
findings.quote: A total unidentified savings requirement of £2.1m is remaining to be achieved over the MTFS period

findings.paper_title: FINAL - Cabinet Treasury Management Outturn Report 2025-26
findings.headline: General Fund capital expenditure was £6.7m against a budget of £32.0m — a 79% underspend
findings.detail: The council budgeted £31.998m for General Fund capital expenditure in 2025/26 but spent only £6.696m. This material variance is presented as an outturn figure without explanation of whether it represents deferred projects, revised capital plans, or other factors affecting the capital programme.
findings.matters: Lenders and finance directors need to understand whether capital programmes are being delivered as planned, as this affects service delivery, infrastructure investment, and the council's financial trajectory.
findings.figures: General Fund capital expenditure: budgeted £31,998k, actual £6,696k (21% of budget)
findings.quote: Capital expenditure · General Fund 7,532 31,998 6,696

findings.paper_title: FINAL - Financial Monitoring Outturn 2025.26 Cabinet Report
findings.headline: £1.022m in assets written down to revenue due to lack of project progress
findings.detail: Both General Fund (£0.509m for old civic zone) and HRA (£0.513m for development sites) had to write down Assets Under Construction to revenue in 2025/26 'due to the lack of progress on the sites'. Document notes expenditure 'served a dual purpose of maintaining the site in its current form and informing the future strategy', suggesting sunk costs with no asset output.
findings.matters: Asset write-downs indicate project management failures and capital allocation errors; suggests governance weaknesses in capital investment decisions
findings.figures: £0.509m General Fund write-down (old civic zone); £0.513m HRA write-down (development sites)
findings.quote: due to the lack of progress on the site, there is no asset at this point in time, so expenditure has been written down to revenue and in 25.26. This is an adverse movement of £0.509m in 2025/26.

findings.paper_title: FINAL - Financial Monitoring Outturn 2025.26 Cabinet Report
findings.headline: Planning income surplus driven by one-off factors unlikely to sustain
findings.detail: Planning income surplus of £0.682m included 'a flurry of land charges application in the final quarter of the year to avoid a law change from 1st April 2026', which artificially boosted income. The report notes this was 'over prudent forecasting' and that income 'continued to perform at a much higher level than seen in previous financial years', but tone suggests caution. Budget increased by £300k for 2026/27 but Finance will 'work with the service to improve forecasting'.
findings.matters: If planning income falls back to historical norms, General Fund surplus could be significantly reduced; reliance on volatile income sources for financial balance is a risk
findings.figures: £0.682m planning income surplus for 2025/26; £0.395m favourable movement from Q3 forecast
findings.quote: There was also a flurry of land charges application in the final quarter of the year to avoid a law change from 1st April 2026, which contributed to the income surplus... Finance will work with the service to improve forecasting planning income in 2026/27

findings.paper_title: FINAL - Financial Monitoring Outturn 2025.26 Cabinet Report
findings.headline: HRA disrepair and damp/mould legal claims expected to continue into 2026/27
findings.detail: The report flags 'increased insurance premiums' and states 'Insurance and legal costs, driven by claims relating to water ingress, damp and mould are also expected to continue into 2026/27.' A pressure of £0.419m was realized against a Q3 forecast of £0.400m. This represents an ongoing liability area.
findings.matters: Ongoing litigation for housing defects creates both immediate cost liability and reputational risk; continuation into 2026/27 suggests systemic housing quality issues unresolved
findings.figures: £0.419m insurance and uninsured losses pressure in 2025/26; includes decant payments and damp/mould losses
findings.quote: Insurance and legal costs, driven by claims relating to water ingress, damp and mould are also expected to continue into 2026/27.

findings.paper_title: FINAL - Financial Monitoring Outturn 2025.26 Cabinet Report
findings.headline: Capital programme slippage of £34.185m signals delivery challenges across major schemes
findings.detail: General Fund slippage of £25.071m includes Leisure (£13.445m), Commercially Sensitive Schemes (£4.006m with DIP investment plan 'still in progress'), and Fleet (£2.29m). HRA slippage of £9.114m includes Paradise Depot development delayed to 2026/27. This represents 36% of the £95.975m original capital budget.
findings.matters: Large capital slippage indicates project management or delivery challenges; deferred investment creates timing mismatches between revenue budgets and capital spend
findings.figures: £25.071m General Fund slippage; £9.114m HRA slippage; total £34.185m out of £95.975m original budget (35.6%)
findings.quote: General Fund Capital is reporting slippage of £25.071m in the General Fund Capital Programme, an increase of £0.426m since Quarter 3. The HRA Capital Programme is reporting slippage of £9.114m, an increase of £2.375m since Quarter 3.

findings.paper_title: FINAL - Financial Monitoring Outturn 2025.26 Cabinet Report
findings.headline: Fleet maintenance pressure of £0.562m continues from prior year and is set to remain in medium term
findings.detail: Fleet repair costs have persisted as a pressure from 2024/25 (£0.327m reported that year). Capital replacement programme has slipped £2.29m to late 2026/27/early 2027/28 due to management vacancies and 18-month manufacturing lead times. The document states this pressure 'is set to remain in the medium term'.
findings.matters: Deferred fleet replacement prolongs expensive repair cycles and suggests capital delivery challenges; medium-term forecast of continued pressure indicates this is structural, not a one-off
findings.figures: £0.562m pressure in 2025/26; £0.327m pressure in 2024/25; £2.29m capital slippage on fleet replacement
findings.quote: The pressure against the Council's management of its Fleet has persisted from 2024/25, with a total pressure of £0.327m for 2025/26... although this pressure is set to remain in the medium term.

findings.paper_title: FINAL - Financial Monitoring Outturn 2025.26 Cabinet Report
findings.headline: Persistent waste service staffing crisis persisting from prior year with £0.268m ongoing agency cost pressure
findings.detail: Agency costs for environmental services sickness have carried over from 2024/25 and remain a ongoing pressure. The report notes 'HGV drivers are very hard to fill' and this is 'a national trend', leaving the council exposed to staffing volatility in a statutory frontline service. The service has 'very little flexibility'.
findings.matters: Chronic reliance on agency staff for statutory services indicates recruitment/retention problems and creates cost volatility in an area where the council cannot reduce service
findings.figures: £0.268m pressure from prior-year sickness cover continuing in 2025/26
findings.quote: Cost pressures caused by agency cover for staff sickness in environmental services persisted from previous years, £0.268m... The service is always subject to the need of agency staff... the staff pool available to deliver the service has very little flexibility and HGV drivers are very hard to fill. This is a national trend.

findings.paper_title: FINAL - Financial Monitoring Outturn 2025.26 Cabinet Report
findings.headline: Business rates funding now at safety net with no growth expected for three years
findings.detail: Dacorum has reached 'safety net level for funding from NNDR', meaning the council receives the minimum guaranteed funding regardless of local economic performance. The report explicitly states 'business rates growth is not expected to be seen over the next 3 years', capping a major revenue source.
findings.matters: Safety net level restricts future financial flexibility; the council cannot benefit from economic growth in its area for three years, limiting revenue-side options if pressures emerge
findings.figures: £5m additional grant funding for business rates relief and safety net received in 2025/26; £3.5m expected to be drawn from FER reserve in 2027/28
findings.quote: The revaluations and empty rates mean that Dacorum are now at safety net level for funding from NNDR. The impact of these changes is likely to mean that business rates growth is not expected to be seen over the next 3 years.

findings.paper_title: FINAL - Financial Monitoring Outturn 2025.26 Cabinet Report
findings.headline: Commercial property portfolio income permanently downwardly revised as targets recognized as unachievable
findings.detail: The portfolio generated a £0.285m pressure against target in 2025/26. The council has now formally recognized that 'current income targets are very unlikely to be achieved in the coming years' and reduced them in the 2026/27 budget. This represents a permanent structural decline in a key income stream.
findings.matters: Income-generating assets that underperform their business case reduce financial flexibility and may indicate weaker property market position than assumed
findings.figures: £0.285m pressure against target; net position after service charge reconciliation and rent reviews
findings.quote: The commercial property portfolio is reporting a net pressure of circa £0.285m against its income target at outturn... It is recognised that current income targets are very unlikely to be achieved in the coming years, so they have been reduced in the 2026/27 budget.

findings.paper_title: FINAL - Financial Monitoring Outturn 2025.26 Cabinet Report
findings.headline: HRA repair and maintenance demand is the council's biggest ongoing financial risk
findings.detail: The report repeatedly emphasizes that demand for repairs and maintenance to council housing stock represents the greatest threat to HRA financial sustainability. Despite a £1.036m underspend on void works in 2025/26, this is attributed to lower Category 3 work rather than lower overall demand, and the report flags this as the area 'most unlikely to be achieved in the coming years' in terms of budget certainty.
findings.matters: If the HRA cannot control maintenance costs on a £63m capital programme, it threatens the council's core housing landlord function and could require General Fund subsidy
findings.figures: £1.036m underspend on void works in 2025/26; cases fell from 459 (2023/24) to 376 (2025/26)
findings.quote: Despite coming in under budget in 2025/26, the demand for repairs and maintenance to Council Homes represents the biggest ongoing risk for the financial sustainability of the Council's housing landlord function.

findings.headline: General Fund working balance maintained at £2.5m (10% of net services), mid-range of 5-15% target
findings.detail: The council maintains a General Fund working balance (contingency reserve) of £2.5m by end of 2026/27, representing approximately 10% of Net Cost of Services (£24.6m). This sits at the midpoint of the council's target range (5-15%). A risk assessment (Appendix J2) confirms this level is appropriate to cover short-term financial issues. The working balance provides adequate but not generous resilience against unforeseen events or budget shortfalls.
findings.matters: Working balance is the primary liquidity reserve and indicator of financial resilience. At 10%, it is adequate for normal operations but provides limited buffer to absorb concurrent shocks (e.g., waste overspend, commercial property income loss, and temp accommodation surge occurring simultaneously).
findings.figures: £2.5m working balance; represents 10% of £24.6m net cost of services; council target range 5-15%
findings.quote: The proposed budget forecasts a General Fund Working Balance of £2.5m by the end of 2025/27, which equates to just over 10% of the Net Cost of Services of £24.6m, as shown in Appendix A1.

findings.headline: Temporary accommodation demand growing as homelessness continues, despite in-budget 2026/27
findings.detail: Temporary accommodation is identified as a "growing pressure" with the service projecting future growth requirements in housing unit volumes needed. For 2026/27, the service is in-budget for the first time in recent years (improvement on prior overspends). A programme of work is underway to support service improvements, and additional homelessness prevention grant is available. However, the trajectory is clearly upward, indicating the council expects continued or accelerating demand for temporary accommodation driven by broader housing and homelessness pressures.
findings.matters: Homelessness and temporary accommodation are statutory services with demand-driven costs. This is a demographic/social pressure that will likely require ongoing budget increases. The current in-budget position masks an underlying demand growth trend that could create future budget pressures or require service contraction.
findings.figures: Service in-budget for 2026/27 (first time in recent years, improvement); growth requirements projected; additional homelessness prevention grant available
findings.quote: Temporary Accommodation is a growing pressure with the service projecting future growth requirements in the volume of units the council has access to, to meet future demand. In year the service is projecting to budget which is an improvement on recent years. There is a programme of work underway to support service improvements, and additional homelessness prevention grant available to support the service requirements.

findings.headline: Waste service faces multiple unresolved structural cost pressures despite transformation efforts
findings.detail: The refuse collection service is flagged as high-risk with multiple structural cost drivers: increased demand for waste routes, rising volumes of collection and disposal, and growing staffing costs. The council is undertaking "constant review and transformation" to reduce waste revenue pressures and expand the commercial waste service, but no specific savings or solutions are quantified in 2026/27. Government policy changes (simpler recycling policy) are expected to add further operational challenges. Performance will be reported quarterly to members if it diverges from budget expectations.
findings.matters: Waste is a statutory service and material operational cost. Multiple unresolved cost drivers with transformation still underway suggest material risk of in-year overspend or future budget pressure. This is both an operational efficiency risk and a service delivery risk.
findings.figures: High-risk area with multiple pressures identified; no specific figures quantified in budget; service flagged for constant review and transformation
findings.quote: There are a multitude of pressures in the refuse service including increased demand for waste routes, increased volumes of waste collection/disposal and the ongoing issues around growing staffing costs. The Governments simpler recycling policy will also no doubt bring challenges and service pressures. The service is under constant review and transformation to reduce ongoing waste revenue pressures and deliver improvements and expansion of the commercial waste service.

findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation creates £1m+ annual transition cost running to April 2028
findings.detail: Dacorum is undergoing local government reorganisation, with transition concluding April 2028. The 2026/27 budget allocates £500k revenue and £500k from the LGR reserve (£1m total). The medium-term financial plan reserves average £1m per annum to support the full programme through 2028. Identified risks include district council recruitment and retention concerns, service/contractual disruption, and ongoing transitional implementation costs. The Hertfordshire councils are developing a 2-year delivery programme to meet government timetable, but detailed resource requirements are still being defined.
findings.matters: LGR creates a contingent structural cost of ~£1m annually for 2+ years that will constrain discretionary spending or require reserve drawdown. Recruitment/retention risks and service disruption during transition could escalate this. This is a material structural change affecting service delivery and financial planning through 2028.
findings.figures: £500k revenue + £500k reserve in 2026/27; average £1m per annum reserved in medium-term plan; programme concludes April 2028; identified risks include recruitment/retention and contractual impacts
findings.quote: At present the 26/27 budget provides a combination of revenue £500k (As detailed in section 7) and the LGR reserve of £500k to support the projected Dacorum contribution. The Dacorum revised Medium Term Financial Plan provides for an average of £1m per annum to be available on the medium term to support this programme

findings.headline: Business rates reset ends Hertfordshire pooling arrangement, removing historical growth upside
findings.detail: The major reset of business rates in 2026/27 eliminates the Hertfordshire business rates pooling arrangement, which previously allowed the council to benefit from business rates growth in strong years. Hertfordshire councils have decided not to operate a pool for 2026/27, and Dacorum is not budgeting for business rates growth. The baseline is being fully reset (baseline ~£78m in 2025/26), and Dacorum's retained amount is set at £3.8m in 2026/27. This removes a source of revenue volatility and upside but increases exposure to downside risk without pooling protection.
findings.matters: Business rates are cyclical and volatile. Loss of pooling protection means the council must absorb all future downside loss on a sector-wide reset. The final retained amount and baseline post-reset are not yet confirmed.
findings.figures: Retained business rates £3.8m in 2026/27; baseline ~£78m in 2025/26 (to be reset in 2026/27); no pooling arrangement; no budget for business rates growth 2026/27
findings.quote: The major reset of the business rates for 26/27 has removed the likelihood of any potential benefit from business rates pooling, and hence like most authorities Hertfordshire have decided not to operate a business rates pool for 2026/27, or budget for growth in 2026/27.

findings.headline: Commercial property portfolio income declining by £400k as cost-of-living pressures reduce occupancy and rents
findings.detail: Budget reduces commercial property portfolio income by £400k in 2026/27 due to economic headwinds. The council explicitly identifies this as a high-risk area where cost-of-living pressures and slow economic growth are reducing demand for commercial properties, making income targets "increasingly challenging." Income-generating services deliver over £15m towards overall service costs, making property income material to the budget. The service is flagged for ongoing scrutiny with quarterly reporting to members if performance diverges from expectations.
findings.matters: Commercial property investment is a material revenue source. A decline signals economic headwinds affecting the council's asset portfolio and occupancy rates. This is a leading indicator of broader economic stress that could cascade to other income streams (parking, planning fees, leisure contracts).
findings.figures: £400k decrease in commercial property income budgeted for 2026/27; income-generating services overall provide £15m+ towards service delivery costs
findings.quote: The impact of the wider economic pressures due to a combination of the impact of the current cost of living pressures and the ongoing slow economic growth is reducing demand on commercial properties and hence commercial property income targets are increasingly challenging.

findings.headline: Pension fund improvement to 106% enables £1.35m annual cost reduction and £650k employer rate cut
findings.detail: The 2025 triennial pension review found the Hertfordshire pension fund significantly improved since 2022, with funding level now 112% sector-wide. Dacorum's funding level improved to 106% (up 5 percentage points since 2022), driven by asset performance exceeding liability growth and updated actuarial assumptions. The council can now cease its secondary contribution (£1.35m annual top-up payment) and reduce the primary employer contribution rate from 19.5% to 17.1%, saving £650k per annum. These are structural improvements to the council's long-term cost base.
findings.matters: Pension cost reduction is a genuine structural improvement to the council's financial sustainability. However, the next triennial review is in 2027, and pension funding is asset-dependent; a market downturn could reverse this improvement.
findings.figures: Dacorum pension fund funding level 106% (up 5% since 2022), Hertfordshire sector level 112% (up 6%); primary employer rate reduction from 19.5% to 17.1%, saving £650k per annum; secondary contribution removal £1.35m; total saving £1.35m by 2027/28
findings.quote: The funding level for Dacorum is provisionally set at 106% an improvement on 2022 of 5%. On the basis of this provisional performance report the actuary have made 2 proposals that will provide significant savings to Dacorum; A reduction in the primary contribution rate that employers pay into the fund from 19.5% to 17.1%. A saving of £650k p.a. Removal of the secondary contribution level paid by Dacorum to top up the pension fund of £1.35m.

findings.headline: Treasury income windfall of £2.2m in 2026/27 declining as cash balances fall from £76m to £25m by 2028
findings.detail: The council has benefited from higher interest rates and maintained strong cash balances, achieving £4m interest income in 2024/25 at an average return of 4.01%. The 2026/27 budget assumes an additional £2.2m income above MTFS assumptions, based on maintaining £68m–£76m cash balances. However, cash flow forecasts project balances declining to £68m by 2027 and £25m by 2028, at which point this treasury benefit ends. This temporary boost supports the headline balanced position but masks a structural income cliff in 2028/29.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand the medium-term run-rate revenue position after this temporary income stream ends. The budget is not self-sustaining without the treasury boost or continued high cash holdings, which are being consumed by capital investment.
findings.figures: £2.2m additional income 2026/27, £1.2m in 2027/28, falling to zero 2028/29; cash balances £100m+ historically, £76m projected 2025/26, £68m by 2027, £25m by 2028; interest income £4m in 2024/25 at 4.01% average rate
findings.quote: The projected cash flow for 2026/27 and 2027/28 shows that cash balances are projected to reduce to year end balances of £68m in 2027 and £25m in 2028. Although there is a significant reduction in the Council's cash balances the treasury still forecasts to exceed current medium term financial planning assumptions in 26/27 and 27/28 with this benefit expected to end in 2028/29.

findings.headline: Dacorum Development Reserve to decline from £4.4m to £0.6m over four years
findings.detail: The Dacorum Development Reserve is planned to decline significantly from £4.394m to £2.280m in 2025/26 (a draw of £2.114m in year 1 alone), then continue declining each year to £609k by 2028/29. This represents an 86% depletion of the reserve over the forecast period.
findings.matters: A capital/development reserve being rapidly depleted suggests either significant capital projects underway or that the council is using this reserve to fund activities. The declining balance threatens future development capacity without external borrowing.
findings.figures: Dacorum Development Reserve declines from £4,394k (2025) to £2,280k (2026) to £609k (2029); year 1 net draw of £1,368k

findings.headline: Leisure Reserve shows unusual spike of £10.79m inflow followed by major drawdowns
findings.detail: The Leisure Reserve shows a net movement of +£10.791m in 2025/26 (increasing from £373k to £11.164k), followed by a draw of (£1.300m) in 2026/27, then a major draw of (£9.400m) in 2027/28, leaving only £287k by 2028/29. This volatile pattern—a large one-off inflow followed by significant outflows—is unusual for normal reserve movements.
findings.matters: Reserves are built gradually for specific purposes; this pattern suggests either an accounting adjustment, a one-off leisure facility funding issue, or an accounting restatement that requires future reversal or funding.
findings.figures: Leisure Reserve movements: +£10,791k (2025/26), then (£1,300k) in 2026/27 and (£9,400k) in 2027/28

findings.headline: Inflationary Pressures Reserve entirely exhausted in 2025/26
findings.detail: The Inflationary Pressures Reserve of £1.048m is planned to be completely drawn in 2025/26 with a net movement of (£1.048m), leaving a zero balance. This reserve was established to provide a buffer against inflation impacts, and its complete depletion in a single year shows those pressures are material.
findings.matters: The council created this reserve specifically to cushion inflation impacts; complete exhaustion shows inflation is materially eating into the budget with no remaining cushion for future pressures.
findings.figures: £1,048k Inflationary Pressures Reserve completely consumed in 2025/26; balance moves from £1,048k to £0
findings.quote: Inflationary Pressures Reserve 1048 0 (1,048) (1,048) 0 0 0 0

findings.headline: Funding Equalisation Reserve being drawn by £7.69m in 2025/26 to balance budget
findings.detail: The largest reserve at £11.953m is planned to have a net movement of (£7.690m) in 2025/26, reducing it to £4.263m. This is 64% of the reserve consumed in a single year. The reserve is then gradually rebuilt with a positive movement of £2.430m in 2026/27, but this shows heavy reliance on a one-off source to balance the current year's budget.
findings.matters: Substantial planned draw from an equalisation reserve to balance the budget indicates the council is not covering its costs from normal revenue and is using reserves to plug a budget gap.
findings.figures: £7,690k net movement out in 2025/26; reserve balance moves from £11,953k to £4,263k
findings.quote: Funding Equalisation Reserve 11953 0 (7,690) (7,690) 4,263 2,430 0 2,430

findings.paper_title: FINAL - Housing Revenue Account Business Plan 2026 Update - FINAL
findings.headline: Arrears and bad debt risk from cost of living pressures; council implementing early intervention
findings.detail: The council acknowledges that the cost of living crisis creates significant risk of increased rent arrears. The HRA Business Plan includes a bad debt provision of 0.79% of gross income and a voids allowance of 0.95%, with mitigation through debt advice, early intervention with households, and support with benefits claims. However, the council notes this is an area where "additional resources will be required to deal with debt recovery and additional support to our tenants."
findings.matters: Cost of living driven arrears directly reduce HRA revenue and increase bad debt costs. If arrears rise beyond the 0.79% provision, the council will need to either find offsetting savings or draw reserves. This is a live economic risk beyond the council's control.
findings.figures: Bad debt provision: 0.79% of gross income; voids allowance: 0.95% of gross income; contribution to bad debt provision: £500k per annum (from Table 2)
findings.quote: The potential impact of the increase in the cost of living could be significant on the number of households in arrears and levels of rent arrears could increase. As a result of this, it is likely that additional resources will be required to deal with debt recovery and additional support to help our tenants.

findings.paper_title: FINAL - Housing Revenue Account Business Plan 2026 Update - FINAL
findings.headline: Government rent convergence consultation response awaited; impact to HRA income not yet modelled
findings.detail: The government launched a consultation in summer 2025 on rent convergence, which would allow rents for properties below 'formula rent' to increase above the CPI+1% cap until they reach formula rent. The government response is expected in January 2026 (the planning document appears dated for early 2026). The business plan explicitly states "Rent Convergence Not included. Awaiting further guidance." This means the financial projections do not yet account for a potentially material change in rent income.
findings.matters: Pending government policy could change rent income permissible under regulation. If unfavourable to Dacorum, it could constrain revenue. If favourable, financial projections may be conservative. The uncertainty means the plan is interim pending policy clarification.
findings.figures: Current rent increase assumption is 4.8% for 2026/27 (CPI+1%); rent convergence impact not quantified
findings.quote: The Government launched a consultation over the summer 2025 on rent convergence, which would allow rents for properties below 'formula rent' to increase above the CPI +1% limit , until they reach formula rent. The Government will provide a response to the consultation in January , detailing how this will be delivered in future years.

findings.paper_title: FINAL - Housing Revenue Account Business Plan 2026 Update - FINAL
findings.headline: Dacorum Investment Partnership launched with developer partner Hill to deliver ~230 homes from 2026/27
findings.detail: A 50:50 long-term strategic partnership between Dacorum and developer Hill was approved by Cabinet in July 2025. The DIP business plan is expected to go to Cabinet in February 2026 (timing in document). The partnership targets start on site on two schemes in 2026/27 with approximately 230 units initially, shifting from project-by-project delivery to a programmed approach. This represents a material change in the council's development model and delivery capacity.
findings.matters: A new strategic partnership with private developer changes governance, risk distribution, and delivery capacity. The council is relying on this partnership to increase affordable housing supply, but performance and financial viability of the joint venture are now shared with an external partner rather than fully controlled.
findings.figures: ~230 units expected initially from 2026/27; total new build programme £62.8m up to 2028/29
findings.quote: Following a Strategic Asset Review the Dacorum Investment Partnership (DIP) – a 50:50 long-term strategic partnership between the Council and development partner Hill and was approved by Cabinet in July 2025. The DIP is currently developing its first business plan – expected to go to Cabinet for approval in February 2025. The business plan will propose opportunities for delivery across several key sites and will target start on site on two schemes in 2026/27, where it is anticipated around 230 units will be delivered initially.

findings.paper_title: FINAL - Housing Revenue Account Business Plan 2026 Update - FINAL
findings.headline: Regulatory judgement below target: C2 rating issued August 2024, target is C1
findings.detail: The Regulator of Social Housing inspected Dacorum in May 2024 and issued a C2 grading in August 2024. The council has developed a Regulatory Action Plan to address areas for improvement and is meeting regularly with the regulator. While a foundation to build on, this rating is below the council's aspiration for a C1 grading, which would demonstrate effective delivery of consumer standards.
findings.matters: A below-target regulatory grade signals compliance gaps in tenant satisfaction, safety, quality, transparency and community standards. This drives mandatory improvement costs and affects the council's reputation as a landlord, relevant to assessing management capability.
findings.figures: C2 grading issued August 2024; council received initial inspection May 2024
findings.quote: Dacorum Borough Council received a C2 grading in our Regulatory Judgement, published in August 2024. Our aspiration is to work towards a future C1 grading, this grading would demonstrate that we, as a landlord, are delivering the outcomes of the consumer standards.

findings.paper_title: Appendix J2 - Working Balance Risk Assessment
findings.headline: The council is including commercial income from service charges as part of its General Fund funding and has identified specific risk here.
findings.detail: Dacorum charges for certain services and has built a commercial income target into its budget to support the overall General Fund position. It has allocated £0.2m of working balance to cover the risk that this income does not materialise.
findings.matters: Service charge income can be more volatile than tax income and may reflect changes in demand or service take-up; failure to deliver this income would require drawing on reserves.
findings.figures: £0.2m provision (1% of commercial income targets)
findings.quote: The Council charges for certain services that it provides and includes a target for this income to support the overall General Fund position.  The working balance provides for risk to delivery of this income.

findings.paper_title: Appendix J2 - Working Balance Risk Assessment
findings.headline: Dacorum is targeting over £3m in investment income for 2026/27, representing a material reliance on financial returns.
findings.detail: The council's General Fund budget includes a specific target for investment income of more than £3m to support service delivery. It has allocated £0.4m of working balance to cover the risk that interest rates or cash balances fall short of forecast.
findings.matters: A significant drop in interest rates or available cash to invest could require budget reductions unless the council increases reserves or cuts other spending.
findings.figures: £3m+ investment income target; £0.4m provision (15% of available balances)
findings.quote: The General Fund has an investment income target of over £3m supporting delivery of Council services in 26/27.  There is provision within the working balance in the event interest rates and cash balances are lower than forecast.

findings.paper_title: Appendix J2 - Working Balance Risk Assessment
findings.headline: The council's 2026/27 budget requires savings, and working balance includes provision for delivery risk.
findings.detail: Dacorum is building savings proposals into its 2026/27 budget and has allocated £0.2m of its working balance specifically to cover the risk that these savings do not materialise fully. This indicates the council has identified specific areas where it needs to reduce spending.
findings.matters: If the council fails to deliver its planned savings, it will need to draw on reserves, potentially eroding its financial flexibility.
findings.figures: £0.2m provision (15% of 26/27 savings requirement)
findings.quote: The budget for 2026/27 includes savings proposals required for the delivery of a balanced budget.   There is provision within the working balance in the event these savings are not delivered in full.

findings.paper_title: Appendix B1 General Fund Change Analysis
findings.headline: Utility cost pressure is identified as a discrete growth item, signalling energy cost headwind
findings.detail: Under premises inflation and growth, £167k is explicitly flagged as 'Utility Cost Pressure' as a growth item rather than routine inflation. This suggests the council has forecast energy costs rising faster than general inflation.
findings.matters: Utility cost volatility is a known pressure on council budgets; this line shows Dacorum is exposed and has already accounted for it in budget planning
findings.quote: Utility Cost Pressure Various 167

findings.paper_title: Appendix B1 General Fund Change Analysis
findings.headline: A £6.3m leisure services movement is described as 'expenditure offset by income' but the detail is opaque
findings.detail: The 'Leisure Agency Agreement - Increase Expenditure Offset by Increased Income' line appears in both the Premises budget (+£6,258k) and the Income section (-£6,258k). This is the single largest movement in the budget and is effectively neutral in terms of net cost, but the structure obscures what is actually happening operationally with leisure provision.
findings.matters: Large budget movements that are described as 'offset' can hide service pressures or commercial risks; a finance director needs visibility on what leisure income assumption is underpinning this and whether it is at risk
findings.figures: £6,258k in expenditure + £6,258k in income offset
findings.quote: Leisure Agency Agreement - Increase Expenditure Offset by Increased Income 6,258

findings.paper_title: Appendix B1 General Fund Change Analysis
findings.headline: Insurance premium renewals are driving cost growth across multiple budget lines
findings.detail: Insurance renewal costs appear in at least four places: Deputy S151 (£26k), premises (£598k), transport (£50k), and an additional £520k recharge to HRA for insurance. The largest single growth item in premises is insurance renewal at £598k. This is aggregate cost pressure that is visible but spread across line items.
findings.matters: Insurance cost inflation is a pressure councils cannot directly control; rising premiums crowd out service delivery. A finance director is tracking whether reserves can absorb this or whether services must be cut.
findings.figures: £26k + £598k + £50k + £520k = £1,194k across identified insurance renewals
findings.quote: Insurance Premium Renewal HO Financial Services (Deputy S151) 26; Insurance Premium Renewal HO Financial Services 598; Insurance Premium Renewal HO Financial Services 50; Insurance Premium - Recharge of HRA Element HO Financial Services (520)

findings.paper_title: Appendix B1 General Fund Change Analysis
findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation is creating £500k of one-off transition and retention costs
findings.detail: The budget flags £250k for 'Short Term Recruitment and Retention Pressures Linked to LGR' and a separate £250k 'LGR Transitional Budget'. This indicates the council is undergoing structural reorganisation that is creating both operational churn and specific transition costs that sit outside normal running.
findings.matters: LGR reshapes council operations and balance sheets; it is material to financial planning and service continuity for both finance leadership and lenders assessing stability
findings.figures: £250k retention pressures + £250k transitional budget = £500k total one-off impact
findings.quote: Short Term Recruitment and Retention Pressures Linked to LGR Chief Executive 250; LGR Transitional Budget Chief Executive 250

findings.paper_title: Appendix B1 General Fund Change Analysis
findings.headline: HRA desrepair legal cases are drawing down resources and generating cross-charging
findings.detail: The council is adding £112k of legal resource in the General Fund specifically to support HRA desrepair cases, and then recharging £112k of that cost back to the HRA. This signals ongoing litigation or settlement activity around housing stock condition. External audit and lenders track council housing liabilities closely.
findings.matters: HRA desrepair liability can scale and land on reserves or borrowing if not managed; a finance director needs to know when legal costs are rising
findings.figures: £112k legal resource addition; £112k recharge to HRA
findings.quote: Legal Resource to Support the HRA With Desrepair Cases HO Legal & Democratic 112

findings.headline: General Fund capital funding exhausts internal resources by 2028/29, requiring £8.271m external borrowing that year
findings.detail: The capital programme shows the General Fund using internal borrowing (reserves drawdown) of £14.614m in 2027/28 and £10.386m in 2028/29, then switching to external borrowing of £8.271m in 2028/29 and £1.740m in 2029/30. This signals the depletion of discretionary reserves and dependence on external markets for capital funding.
findings.matters: This shows the timeline and scale of when the council's financial flexibility ends. Inability to access external markets or rising interest rates would then constrain the capital programme.
findings.figures: Internal Borrowing-General Fund £14.614m (2027/28), £10.386m (2028/29); External Borrowing-General Fund £8.271m (2028/29), £1.740m (2029/30)
findings.quote: Internal Borrowing- General Fund 0.000 0.000 14.614 10.386 0.000 [and] External Borrowing- General Fund 0.000 0.000 0.000 8.271 1.740 [from capital programme financing table]

findings.headline: £69.342m investment property portfolio generating £4.37m net income is material to achieving budget targets
findings.detail: The council holds £69.342m in investment properties (shops, industrial units, offices, filling stations) generating £5.09m gross and £4.37m net income. This net income is explicitly stated as helping deliver the £15.565m net expenditure target for 2025/26. Loss of rental income or property values would directly impact the general fund budget.
findings.matters: A lender assesses income concentration risk and asset quality. A finance director must plan for any deterioration in occupancy rates, rents, or property values. The council's budget targets depend on sustaining this income stream.
findings.figures: £69.342m portfolio value, £5.09m gross income, £4.37m net income, £15.565m net expenditure before council tax
findings.quote: At the 31st March 2025, the Statement of Accounts showed the Council held £69.342m of Investment Properties... The net income from Investment Properties is £4.37m, which helps contribute to a lower net expenditure before Council Tax.

findings.headline: HRA external borrowing begins at £34.455m in 2026/27 to replace internal borrowing, alongside £12.674m annual interest on Self Financing debt
findings.detail: The council is switching HRA capital financing from internal borrowing (£28.264m in 2025/26) to external borrowing (£34.455m starting 2026/27), continuing at £31-33m annually through 2029/30. This coincides with fixed interest charges of £12.674m per year on the £354m Self Financing deal, creating substantial fixed HRA obligations.
findings.matters: This move to external markets exposes the council to refinancing risk and market rates. Combined with the £12.674m annual interest, this constrains HRA flexibility to invest in stock improvements or management. A lender needs to ensure HRA rental income covers these fixed costs.
findings.figures: Internal Borrowing-HRA £28.264m (2025/26) falls to £0; External Borrowing-HRA £34.455m, £33.727m, £31.369m, £31.715m (2026/27-2029/30); interest £12.674m annually
findings.quote: External Borrowing-HRA 0.000 34.455 33.727 31.369 31.715 [from capital programme financing table]; the HRA is required to pay interest on the borrowing undertaken to fund the £354m Self Financing deal. In 2026/27 this is budgeted to be £12.674m.

findings.headline: Gross debt forecast to grow from £331.335m to £416.232m by 2028/29
findings.detail: The council projects total gross debt will increase by approximately £85m over four years. The underlying Capital Financing Requirement grows even faster, from £385.392m to £523.330m, indicating substantial planned capital borrowing. By 2028/29, the council forecasts underborrowing of £107.098m, meaning it will hold reserves rather than borrow.
findings.matters: A lender assesses debt serviceability and trajectory. Rapidly growing debt requires monitoring to ensure it remains manageable within the council's revenue budget, especially when combined with interest and MRP costs.
findings.figures: Gross debt £331.335m (2024/25 actual) to £416.232m (2028/29 estimate); Capital Financing Requirement £385.392m to £523.330m
findings.quote: The Council has total gross debt of £331.335m at the end of 2024/25 and forecasts £523.33m at the end of 2028/29.

findings.headline: Council adopts cautious stance on 2026/27 borrowing, signalling uncertainty on interest rates and timing
findings.detail: The treasury strategy explicitly states 'Caution will be adopted with the 2026/27 treasury operations.' The council will postpone borrowing if rates are expected to fall sharply, or consider fixed-rate borrowing if sharp rises threaten. This signals uncertainty about the interest rate path and suggests borrowing decisions may be delayed.
findings.matters: Uncertainty and delays in borrowing decisions may disrupt capital expenditure timetables, require interim funding arrangements, or lock in higher rates if market conditions worsen.
findings.figures: Bank Rate 3.75% (December 2025); MUFG forecast: rate cut to 3.25% Q4 2026
findings.quote: Caution will be adopted with the 2026/27 treasury operations. The Council will monitor interest rates in financial markets and adopt a pragmatic approach to changing circumstances.  If it was felt there was a significant risk of a sharp fall in borrowing rates, then borrowing may be postponed.

findings.headline: Capital receipts forecast to collapse 89% from £33m to £3.5m by 2028/29, forcing increased borrowing dependency
findings.detail: Capital receipts are projected to fall from £32.806m in 2025/26 to £10.712m in 2027/28 and just £3.549m by 2028/29. This dramatic decline removes a primary source of capital funding and means the council must borrow for nearly all future capital expenditure, substantially increasing leverage.
findings.matters: Collapsing capital receipts (typically from asset sales) force the council into external borrowing to maintain capital programmes, raising debt ratios and reducing the scope to manage debt levels.

findings.headline: Council shifts from internal borrowing to external borrowing for HRA, requiring £34m external debt in 2026/27
findings.detail: The council moves from under-borrowing (using internal cash) to external borrowing. In 2026/27, the financing plan mandates £34.455m of external HRA borrowing, with a further £33.727m, £31.369m, and £31.715m in following years. This marks a structural shift from reserves-funded to market-funded capital investment.
findings.matters: Moving to external markets exposes the council to capital market conditions, interest rate risk, and refinancing risk; the timing and terms of this borrowing will materially affect debt costs and financial sustainability.

findings.headline: Liquid investment balances projected to collapse from £45m to £4m by 2027/28, limiting financial flexibility
findings.detail: Expected treasury investments are forecast to fall from £45.275m in 2025/26 to £40.033m in 2026/27, then sharply to £11.913m and finally £4.321m in 2027/28 before recovering to £15.098m. This severe depletion of liquid resources reflects capital spending outpacing revenue resources and leaves minimal cash buffer.
findings.matters: Depleted liquid reserves significantly constrain the council's ability to absorb unexpected costs, manage seasonal cash flows, or respond to emergencies; it indicates heavy reliance on external borrowing and market access.

findings.headline: Capital Financing Requirement growing 34% to £548m, underlining a massive long-term borrowing need
findings.detail: Total CFR is projected to increase from £408.882m in 2025/26 to £548.123m by 2029/30—an increase of £139m. The HRA CFR accounts for nearly all of this, rising from £391.608m to £498.123m. The council's capital investment programme is substantial and the resulting borrowing requirement will dominate its balance sheet for years.
findings.matters: A growing CFR signals the magnitude of capital commitments ahead and the scale of debt the council will need to service long-term, which directly affects debt affordability and financial sustainability.

findings.headline: HRA debt-to-revenue ratio deteriorates sharply, rising from 526% to 574% across the strategy period
findings.detail: Housing Revenue Account debt grows from £391.61m in 2025/26 to £498.12m by 2029/30, while HRA revenues only rise modestly from £74.381m to £86.773m. The debt-to-revenue ratio worsens from 526% to 574%, and debt per dwelling increases from £39,157 to £49,668. This trajectory shows declining HRA financial sustainability and rising leverage.
findings.matters: An accelerating HRA debt ratio is a primary indicator of financial distress for local authorities; a lender or finance director would view a 574% ratio as indicating significant vulnerability and requiring urgent intervention.
findings.figures: HRA debt 2025/26–2029/30: £391.61m–£498.12m; HRA revenues £74.381m–£86.773m; debt-to-revenue ratio 526%–574%; debt per dwelling £39,157–£49,668

findings.committee: Finance and Resources Overview and Scrutiny
findings.headline: Electric Vehicle Charging Point income growing rapidly with 85% usage increase, but still modest absolute value
findings.detail: EVCP programme nearing completion (2 sites remaining) has generated £47,980 income to date, with usage increasing 85% since January 2025. Projected to continue increasing. This emerging revenue source is aligned with policy trends but remains small relative to overall income.
findings.matters: Shows positive growth in an emerging revenue stream aligned with national policy. However, absolute value remains modest and the full trajectory is uncertain.
findings.figures: £47,980 generated to date, 85% usage increase since January 2025
findings.quote: usage has increased 85% since January '25 and it is projected that income will continue to increase over the next 12 months

findings.committee: Finance and Resources Overview and Scrutiny
findings.headline: Parking and fees increases totalling £118k above MTFS assumptions planned for April 2026
findings.detail: The council is implementing parking permit increases (£25k) and broader fees and charges increases (£93k) from April 2026, beyond inflation already assumed in the Medium-Term Financial Strategy. Parking permit increases specifically start April 2026.
findings.matters: Shows the council raising charges on residents above inflation. This could impact service take-up and demand, and may face political resistance.
findings.figures: £25k from parking permit increases, £93k from other fees and charges review
findings.quote: Parking Permits Increase: Projected to generate an additional £25k. April 2026 ... Fees & Charges Review: Projected income in fees & charges above the MTFS assumed inflation rate

findings.committee: Finance and Resources Overview and Scrutiny
findings.headline: Commercial waste identified as new income stream, diversifying council's commercial portfolio
findings.detail: Commercial waste has been identified and included in the £1.1M new income target at £90k. This represents the council entering a new market rather than optimising existing services, potentially expanding further once the first phase is completed.
findings.matters: Shows the council diversifying its income base away from traditional user charges. However, it also represents expansion into new commercial markets with associated operational and market risks.
findings.figures: £90k projected from commercial waste
findings.quote: Commercial Waste (New Stream): £90k

findings.committee: Finance and Resources Overview and Scrutiny
findings.headline: Garage portfolio repurposing requires significant capital investment with long-term return on investment, creating potential capital and cash-flow risk
findings.detail: Specialist consultancy review of 750 garage sites identified 60 with potential for alternative commercial use. However, repurposing requires significant investment with only long-term ROI. The council is still undertaking financial viability assessments, and completion of analysis is planned for Q4 2025-26.
findings.matters: If pursued, this represents material capital expenditure with delayed and uncertain returns. This affects the council's capital strategy, borrowing requirements and cash-flow timing.
findings.figures: 750 garage sites assessed, 60 identified for repurposing, lowest-performing 25% targeted
findings.quote: Repurposing requires significant investment, and the return on investment (ROI) is likely to be long-term.

findings.committee: Finance and Resources Overview and Scrutiny
findings.headline: £1.1 Million in new commercial income identified and on-track to deliver from parking, garages and new commercial waste service
findings.detail: The Commercial Income Review has identified £1.1M in additional income: £660k from parking, £371k from garages, and £90k from commercial waste. These are described as on-track for delivery, suggesting these targets are embedded in financial planning.
findings.matters: This shows concrete revenue actions to offset government funding reductions. However, delivery is critical—if these targets slip, the council's medium-term financial strategy is at risk.
findings.figures: £1.1 Million total: Parking £660k, Garages £371k, Commercial Waste £90k
findings.quote: Identified and on-track to deliver £1.1 Million in additional income: Parking: £660k Garages: £371k Commercial Waste (New Stream): £90k

findings.committee: Finance and Resources Overview and Scrutiny
findings.headline: Commercial revenue now comprises nearly 50% of total council income, making the Commercial Strategy critical to financial sustainability
findings.detail: The council's financial model has become heavily reliant on commercial activity. The report states this continued revenue is "critical" as government funding reduces and demand for services increases. This concentration of funding in discretionary commercial streams rather than stable baseline government grant represents a structural change to the council's revenue base.
findings.matters: Lenders need to assess the sustainability and resilience of a council's income. Dependency on commercial revenue that can fluctuate with market conditions or operational changes presents different risk to traditional grant funding.
findings.figures: Nearly 50% of total Council income
findings.quote: General Fund commercial revenue accounts for nearly 50% of total Council income.

findings.headline: Strategic Risk Register presented only in Q2 and Q4, not on the required quarterly basis to governance
findings.detail: Council policy requires the Strategic Risk Register to be presented to Cabinet and Audit Committee each quarter. Review of 2024/25 minutes confirms it was only presented in Q2 and Q4. While risks were discussed through alternative risk clinics by the Corporate Leadership Team, formal governance reporting of strategic risks to those charged with oversight was incomplete.
findings.matters: Consistent quarterly reporting of strategic risks to the Audit Committee is essential for effective oversight and early escalation of emerging financial threats. Reporting gaps in governance, even if risks are discussed elsewhere, weaken the control environment and reduce the assurance that critical risks reach appropriate decision-makers.
findings.figures: Presented 2 times in 2024/25 instead of required 4 times
findings.quote: A review of the Cabinet and Audit Committee minutes confirmed that the SRR was only presented in Q2 and Q4 in 2024/25, with no risk reporting in the intervening periods to those groups.

findings.headline: £5.9m correction to pension liabilities after final actuarial report showed actual asset returns exceeded estimates by £5m
findings.detail: The draft financial statements included an estimated return on pension plan assets. The final IAS19 actuarial report revealed actual returns exceeded the estimate by £5,023k, requiring a £5,926k adjustment (plus £906k for asset ceiling effects). This represented 44.9% of the year's Other Comprehensive Income, demonstrating material estimation uncertainty in pension valuations.
findings.matters: Pension liabilities are material to the council's financial position (net liability £18.6m after asset ceiling). Post-close adjustments of this magnitude indicate significant estimation risk; actual pension outcomes diverge materially from assumptions, which lenders need to understand when assessing balance sheet stability.
findings.figures: £5,023k return variance, £5,926k total adjustment, 44.9% of SOCI impact, net pension liability £18.6m
findings.quote: The revision resulted in an increase of £5,023k in the fair value of scheme assets due to the actual return on planned assets exceeding the estimated return on place assets

findings.headline: Auditors report ineffective management controls over valuations of major assets totalling £1.4bn due to council lacking in-house valuation expertise
findings.detail: The auditors identified that management review controls relating to land and buildings (£153.9m), council dwellings (£1,189m), investment property (£69.3m), and post-retirement benefit obligations are ineffective per auditing standards. The Council does not have in-house valuation expertise and relies entirely on external valuers (Wilks Head & Eve for property, Barnett Waddingham for pensions) with no formal internal capability to challenge valuations.
findings.matters: Large asset valuations directly affect the balance sheet and borrowing capacity. Weak controls and lack of in-house expertise, even though no misstatements were found this year, increase the risk that material errors could go undetected in future periods. This represents a structural gap in the control environment.
findings.figures: Land and buildings £153.9m, Council dwellings £1,189m, Investment property £69.3m
findings.quote: The Council lacks a formal control over the valuation of land and buildings to ensure that relevant valuation was appropriate as the Council does not have the relevant in house valuation expertise.

findings.paper_title: Appendix D Final Draft Auditors Annual Report
findings.headline: Strategic Risk Register reporting only occurred in Q2 and Q4, creating governance gaps in Q1 and Q3 scrutiny of risk management
findings.detail: The Strategic Risk Register was reported to the Audit Committee and Cabinet only in Q2 and Q4 of 2024/25, with no formal risk reporting in Q1 and Q3 due to the refresh cycle. While the Corporate Leadership Team conducted risk clinics in intervening periods, the auditor noted that consistent quarterly reporting to Cabinet and Audit Committee is required to ensure appropriate scrutiny and challenge. KPMG raised a performance improvement observation requiring quarterly Strategic Risk Register reporting.
findings.matters: Consistent quarterly risk reporting to governance bodies ensures timely identification and oversight of emerging material risks; gaps in formal reporting to those charged with governance can delay risk escalation and response.
findings.figures: Q1 and Q3 2024/25 with no Strategic Risk Register reporting to Cabinet and Audit Committee
findings.quote: Whilst this ensured a level of challenge was applied to these risks, we would expect the Strategic Risk Register to be reported to the Cabinet and Audit Committee each quarter to ensure appropriate scrutiny and challenge is applied by those charged with governance.

findings.paper_title: Appendix D Final Draft Auditors Annual Report
findings.headline: Temporary accommodation cost pressure resulted in £0.5m overspend in 2024/25, flagged as an emerging financial risk
findings.detail: The Council experienced significant cost pressures relating to its statutory duty to place residents in temporary accommodation, resulting in an overspend of approximately £0.5m in 2024/25. Although this did not place significant strain on overall financial sustainability, it is explicitly identified as an emerging area of risk. The Council has approved an updated Preventing Homelessness & Rough Sleeping Strategy 2024-2029 focused on prevention and is working to optimise the temporary accommodation mix, particularly minimising use of hotels and B&Bs which carry the highest costs.
findings.matters: Temporary accommodation is a statutory obligation with rising cost pressures that could escalate if demand increases; the identified £0.5m overspend represents ongoing financial volatility in a mandatory spend area.
findings.figures: £0.5m overspend on temporary accommodation in 2024/25
findings.quote: Although the Council delivered a balanced budget for 2024/25 and a surplus on both the General Fund and HRA, in common with many other authorities locally and nationally it experienced significant cost pressures relating to the statutory duty to place residents in temporary accommodation. This resulted in an overspend of c£0.5m in 2024/25.

findings.paper_title: Appendix D Final Draft Auditors Annual Report
findings.headline: Housing Regulator identified weaknesses in consumer standards compliance during first inspection, requiring improvements to avoid poor tenant outcomes
findings.detail: The Council was subject to its first inspection by the Regulator of Social Housing focused on consumer standards, receiving a C2 grading (second highest available). The regulator identified weaknesses in the Council's delivery of consumer standard outcomes; improvements are needed to avoid poor outcomes for tenants. The Council has produced and enacted a detailed regulatory action plan currently being implemented and monitored.
findings.matters: The Council owns over 10,000 homes representing 20% of all homes in the borough, making this a material operational responsibility; regulator-identified weaknesses in housing management standards affect service quality and the council's operational risk profile.
findings.figures: Council owns 10,000+ homes; approximately 20% of all homes within the borough; C2 grading (second highest rating available)
findings.quote: The Council was subject to its first inspection by the regulator of social housing, focusing on consumer standard, in which it received a grading of C2. Although this is the second highest available rating, this did mean that the regulator identified some weaknesses in the Council delivering the outcomes of the consumer standards and some improvements are needed in order to avoid poor outcomes for tenants.

findings.headline: Formal bad debt provision policy still missing after three years of audit recommendations
findings.detail: Since at least 2022, auditors have recommended the Council adopt a formal bad debt policy. The Council still relies on professional judgment and cumulative knowledge of debtors. While current provisions appear adequate, this creates inconsistency and exposure to human error across different debtor types. Testing is ongoing on this outstanding item.
findings.matters: Bad debt provisions are a control estimate that affects the bottom line. A formal policy ensures consistency and defensibility of judgment calls across income streams.
findings.figures: Proportion of bad debt policy implementation: still not adopted as of August 2025 review
findings.quote: The Council does not have a formal bad debt policy. The Council prepare the bad debt calculation based on professional judgement and cumulative knowledge of the individuals debtors

findings.headline: Strategic Risk Register not reported quarterly to Cabinet and Audit Committee as policy requires
findings.detail: The Council's risk management policy requires the Strategic Risk Register to be presented to Cabinet and Audit Committee each quarter. In 2024/25 it was only presented in Q2 and Q4. Risks were discussed by senior leadership in intervening periods via 'risk clinics' but those charged with governance did not receive quarterly oversight. KPMG raised this as a 'medium priority performance improvement observation'.
findings.matters: Quarterly risk reporting is a key governance control. Without it, the Council and its lenders lack visibility of how financial and strategic risks are being monitored and escalated by senior management.
findings.figures: Reporting occurred in Q2 and Q4 only, not all four quarters
findings.quote: A review of the Cabinet and Audit Committee minutes confirmed that the SRR was only presented in Q2 and Q4 in 2024/25, with no risk reporting in the intervening periods to those groups

findings.headline: Investment property valuations (£69.3m) also lack formal management review controls
findings.detail: The Council's £69.3m investment property portfolio is valued by external experts but the Council lacks formal in-house valuation expertise and formal controls to challenge the valuers' work. Auditors note management operates an informal control they are satisfied with, but formal controls are absent. Testing is ongoing and no misstatements identified to date.
findings.matters: Investment property valuations are inherently subjective and material to the balance sheet. Weak controls over a £69m asset class create risk of undetected misstatement.
findings.figures: Investment property held at fair value: £69.3m
findings.quote: The Council lacks a formal control over the valuation of investment properties to ensure that relevant valuation was appropriate as the Council does not have the relevant in house valuation expertise

findings.headline: Auditors report management review controls over £1,343.7m of land and buildings valuations are 'ineffective' by audit standards
findings.detail: KPMG found that the Council's control over revalued land and buildings (including £1,189m of council dwellings) is ineffective in design and implementation. The audit notes this is difficult to control given inherent subjectivity in valuations, but highlights the Council lacks a formal control over the valuation process. No material misstatement was identified to date, but this is a significant control weakness.
findings.matters: Land and buildings represent the majority of the Council's asset base. Ineffective controls over their valuation create audit risk and could mask material misstatements in future years.
findings.figures: Land and buildings £153.9m; Council dwellings £1,189m; total property assets £1,343.7m
findings.quote: Auditing standards require us to report that the design and implementation of the management review control relating to this area remains ineffective in line with the ISA definition

findings.headline: £5m uncorrected overstatement of pension asset value awaiting management correction
findings.detail: KPMG identified that management initially used estimated rather than actual returns on pension fund assets. The revised IAS19 report showed actual return on plan assets exceeded the estimate by £5,023k. This adjustment has been identified but not yet corrected in the financial statements—it overstates Other Comprehensive Income by 41.7% and must be corrected before audit sign-off.
findings.matters: This is a material balance sheet error in pension liabilities that affects reserve calculations and must be corrected before accounts are signed. A lender needs confidence the final accounts are accurate.
findings.figures: £5,023k adjustment to pension assets; 41.7% overstatement of Other Comprehensive Income
findings.quote: Testing identified that management had received a revised IAS19 valuation report after production of the accounts. The revision resulted in an increase of £5,023k in the fair value of scheme assets due to the actual return on planned assets exceeding the estimated return on place assets

findings.headline: Procurement Strategy expired in 2024 with no replacement strategy yet in place
findings.detail: The Council's Commissioning and Procurement Strategy covering 2019–2024 has expired. No new strategy exists for 2025 onwards, though management has committed to development over 2025 with formal approval by December 2025. The council is operating under updated Standing Orders but without current strategic procurement direction. The delay was due to prioritizing Procurement Act 2023 implementation.
findings.matters: A lender needs assurance that a council's procurement is operating under a current strategic framework. An expired strategy indicates lack of current strategic direction for commercial decisions.
findings.figures: Strategy covered 2019–2024; new strategy due December 2025
findings.quote: The Council's Commissioning and Procurement Strategy expired in 2024, with no updated strategy yet in place, though new Standing Orders have been approved.

news_drafts.headline: Council tax collection rates declining in Dacorum amid household financial vulnerability.
news_drafts.lead: Declining tax collection reduces actual revenue below forecasts and signals emerging household financial stress that could spread across other councils.

news_drafts.headline: 2027/28 budget balance depends on £900k in unproven efficiencies and income that council flags as at-risk.
news_drafts.lead: Savings plans flagged at-risk but essential to balance the budget indicate execution risk; non-delivery would force mid-year service cuts or reserve drawdown.

news_drafts.headline: Local Government Reorganisation creating structural change with undefined transition costs ahead of July 2026 government decision
news_drafts.lead: Major institutional restructuring creates execution and financial risk; a lender must assess whether this will require additional borrowing or will consume resources that could otherwise support debt service.
